profile.story: Dr. Hannah Cole left family medicine in 2017 and built a Scottsdale med spa on her own hands and her own name. Eight years later the business is $2.01M with nine people, and 78% of injectable revenue is still delivered by her personally — her calendar is booked nine weeks out while her nurse practitioner has three-day availability. She is charting until 9pm most nights, has not taken more than four consecutive days off in two years, and answered the wellbeing question with 'Running on empty.' A second, quieter problem surfaced in Block 5: the 2019 delegation agreement that lets Renata inject under her supervision cannot be found, and aestheticians have occasionally done neurotoxin touch-ups on her verbal direction.

intake.q2: We are a physician-owned medical spa. Injectables are the core — neurotoxin and dermal filler — alongside laser and energy-device treatments, medical-grade facials, a medical weight-management program and retail skincare. Patients are almost all women 34–62 in north Scottsdale and Paradise Valley, roughly 60% of revenue from patients who have been with us more than two years. Everything is delivered in our own four-room suite; I do the injectable work and the clinical oversight, my nurse practitioner covers a share of it, and two licensed aestheticians run the device and facial side.

intake.q5: A practice that fills two injector calendars, not one. Around $2.6M, four rooms running six days, a practice manager who owns the numbers, a second NP or PA, and me in the chair three clinical days a week instead of five — doing the complex cases and the training, not every unit of tox in the building. I would like to be able to leave for two weeks and have the schedule not collapse.

intake.q8: I am the bottleneck. Patients book me by name and will wait nine weeks rather than see my NP, so revenue is capped at whatever I can physically inject in a week. It has been true since about 2022 and it got worse when we added the third room, because now I am the only thing that isn't scalable.

blockNotes.b1: She named the constraint herself before we asked: 'I am the bottleneck.' Nine-week wait on her calendar, three days on Renata's. Answered q57 'Running on empty' without hesitating and then apologised for it. Longest break in twelve months is four days and she charted through it.
blockNotes.b2: 140 inquiries a month, all three channels land in Boulevard — the capture is genuinely good. The leak is after the consult: 48% convert, ~35% get a second touch, and the most common loss reason is the wait for her calendar, not price. Funnel reconciles: 140 × 48% × $740 = ~$597K of first visits, and 1,940 active patients at 3.2 visits a year gets to $2.01M within 12%.
blockNotes.b3: Boulevard tour. Booking, charting, memberships and payments in one system, which is more than most. Then the paper: a printed intake and consent packet, scanned, and the medical history typed back into Boulevard by hand — 25 a day. Watched it happen twice during the tour.
blockNotes.b4: 17.5 h/wk of repetitive work inventoried, 5.4 of it Dr. Cole's own after-clinic charting priced at $210/hr loaded. Nine people, ~340 available hours — the load is 5%, well inside plausible. Kayla is the only person who touches inventory, membership billing or the numbers.
blockNotes.b5: Asked about the delegation agreement and the room changed. The 2019 template could not be produced; she thinks it is in a file at her old accountant's. She also volunteered that aestheticians have done 'a couple of units of touch-up' on her verbal say-so. Told her plainly this is a question for a healthcare attorney licensed in Arizona and that we would not answer it — recorded as an overlay and a referral, not a finding.

P1.note: Sources and rough volumes known — Instagram ~55/mo at $2,400, referral ~38, Google ~30, events ~17. Boulevard captures a source tag only when the front desk remembers to ask; about 40% of bookings carry none.
P1.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs monthly volume actually logged in one place; two out of five bookings have no source at all.

P2.note: Every inquiry — web form, call and Instagram DM — lands in Boulevard with Marisol; shown live on the tour. Response 4–6 hours on clinic days; confirmation text is automated.
P2.why_not_higher: Anchor 4 needs response under an hour and an automated first response; evening DMs wait until the next morning.

P3.note: 'Maybe 35% get a second touch, when Marisol has a gap.' Consults that did not book get a call from memory; nothing after that.
P3.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a defined sequence used on most leads and missed follow-ups visible in the system; there is no sequence and no record.

P4.note: Consult→treatment ~48%, kept as a running tally in Marisol's notebook. No stages in Boulevard. Loss reason recorded anecdotally as price and calendar wait.
P4.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs stages defined and used and a close rate actually tracked in the system.

P5.note: Treatment menu footer dated March 2023 (Doc). One change since: neurotoxin per-unit price up $1 in January 2025 after a vendor increase. Discounts given at the chair at her discretion. q28: 'Pricing is a current worry.'
P5.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs real economics behind prices and occasional reviews; there has been one anecdotal change in two and a half years.

P6.note: Memberships, retail skincare and an unnamed 'lip and tox' pairing get offered when the provider thinks of it. Device series are the only packaged item; no premium tier, no injectable bundle.
P6.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs named tiers or bundles with a scripted upsell on the core offer; nothing is written and nothing is routine.

P7.note: Boulevard dashboard shown live: 71% repeat, 88% membership retention, 214 members. Lapsed memberships get a call. The 780 patients with no visit in 14 months have never been contacted.
P7.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs an inactive list pulled and worked at least twice a year; only membership lapses are touched.

P8.note: Marketing is Dr. Cole plus a 10 h/wk coordinator; sales is Marisol 'informally'; $3,000/mo budget. q30: leads, conversion, CAC and customer value have never been reviewed in the same sitting.
P8.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs named owners and numbers reviewed at least sometimes; the numbers are never reviewed together at all.

P9.note: Gross margin 62% confirmed on the 24-month P&L. The Boulevard export gives revenue by service line but carries no cost, so the 72% injectable margin is Dr. Cole's estimate off vendor invoices.
P9.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs margin by service line known from a record and used in pricing; it is a memory, and the March 2023 menu shows it has not driven a price decision.

P10.note: QuickBooks closes by the 12th (Doc: 24 monthly P&Ls, all dated). Dr. Cole and Kayla review it monthly. One target exists — revenue $2.4M.
P10.why_not_higher: Anchor 4 needs targets across the numbers; q21 shows 'No target' on margin, profit, cash and owner comp.

S1.note: Scheduling, front desk and retail run without her. q50: pricing exceptions, major sales, escalations, hiring, purchasing, quality sign-off, banking, vendors and strategy all return to her. Two clinical escalations arrived on her phone during Block 1.
S1.why_not_higher: Only routine work is delegated; anchor 2 needs several areas genuinely delegated with money and hiring the remaining exception.

S2.note: Four-week test (q51): week one Renata covers ~40% of the injectable book; then new consults stop, controlled-product ordering stops, and nobody decides anything clinical or financial. Longest actual absence in 12 months: four days, worked through.
S2.why_not_higher: Runs about a week and she answers from away; anchor 2 needs it to run short-term with decisions merely stacking up, not revenue stopping.

S3.note: Marisol can quote and book a plan, but Dr. Cole presents and closes everything over $2,500 and 78% of injectable revenue is on her hands. q14: ~70% of revenue tied to her personal relationships.

S4.note: Kayla Ruiz is 14 months into the practice-manager role and owns the schedule and supplies, but escalates anything touching money or a patient complaint. q38: 'Mostly clear, with gaps.' No manager owns a metric.

S5.note: The 2021 injection protocol binder was opened in session: current on technique, silent on consent, complications and post-care. q35: 35% documented, 15% current. New aestheticians learn by shadowing; Boulevard chart templates are used.

S7.note: Quality is her hands — she reviews every before/after photo herself. q31: +20% would need 'equipment or capital', and the injectable book is already nine weeks out. Recurring failures include scheduling delays and 'the owner has to step in'.
S7.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs delivery that is mostly consistent and where growth takes heroics; here growth has physically nowhere to go.

S8.why_not_higher: Top of the anchor. The concentration risk in this business is a person, not a customer — carried on S10 and the key-person overlay.

assessment.owner_objective: Reduce owner dependence — get injectable revenue off one pair of hands without losing the patients who book her by name.
assessment.owner_belief: I am the bottleneck. Patients book me by name and will wait nine weeks rather than see my NP, so revenue is capped at whatever I can physically inject in a week. It has been true since about 2022 and it got worse when we added the third room, because now I am the only thing that isn't scalable.
assessment.primary_constraint: Revenue is capped at the treatment hours of a single licensed provider, because nothing in the practice — the booking flow, the consult script, the price list or the brand — has ever been built to hand a patient to anyone but Dr. Cole.
assessment.constraint_symptoms: Block 1: nine-week wait on her calendar against three days on Renata's, and q57 'Running on empty'. Block 2: the most common loss reason is the wait, not price, and 48% consult conversion is measured only in a notebook. Block 3: the four-week test stops 60% of injectable revenue in week two. Block 5: 78% of injectable revenue and ~70% of all revenue sits on her personal relationships. Four blocks; the rule requires two.
assessment.constraint_cost: ~$186K of injectable revenue turned away or delayed past the nine-week horizon last year (Boulevard waitlist abandonment, Doc) · ~$58K of contribution sitting idle in Renata's unbooked chair at current injectable margin · 281 owner hours a year on after-clinic charting at a $210 loaded rate.
assessment.constraint_fix: Make Renata the default injector for maintenance neurotoxin: a provider-neutral consult script, a Renata-first booking rule with Dr. Cole reserved for filler and complex cases, a written treatment protocol so the standard of care is the practice's and not one person's, and a resolved delegation agreement so the handoff is legally clean before it is operationally real.
assessment.momentum_initiative: Reprice the treatment menu. It has not moved materially since March 2023, it is a decision rather than a project, it is entirely in her control, and it lands in the P&L inside 30 days.

opportunities.title: Reprice the treatment menu — unchanged since March 2023
opportunities.finding: The price list footer reads March 2023 (Doc). The single change since is a $1 per-unit neurotoxin increase in January 2025 that passed through a vendor cost rise and kept nothing. Injectables are 46% of revenue at a 72% margin, the calendar is nine weeks out, and the stated loss reason is wait time rather than price — a demand curve that is not price-sensitive at the top of the book.
opportunities.blueprint: Rebuild the injectable menu from unit cost upward: per-unit toxin and per-syringe filler cost from the vendor invoices, target contribution by line, a written discount rule replacing chair-side discretion, and a one-page 'why' script the whole team can say out loud. Notify members 30 days ahead; hold membership pricing for existing members for one renewal cycle.
opportunities.replaces: Chair-side discounting at the owner's discretion, and a menu that has absorbed two years of product cost increases.

opportunities.title: Reactivate the 780 patients with no visit in 14 months
opportunities.finding: Boulevard holds 1,940 patients seen in the last 24 months; 780 have nothing in the last 14. q27: inactive patients are not identified and no reactivation campaign has ever run. These people already chose the practice once and cost nothing to acquire again.
opportunities.blueprint: Segment the dormant file by last treatment type, write three sequences (tox lapsed, device series unfinished, membership cancelled), route every booking to Renata's calendar by default so recovered demand lands in the open chair rather than the nine-week one, and measure booked-versus-contacted weekly.
opportunities.replaces: Nothing — this list has never been worked.

opportunities.title: Take the paper intake and consent packet off the front desk
opportunities.finding: 25 packets a day are printed, signed, scanned and then re-keyed into the Boulevard chart at 14 minutes each — 5.8 h/wk at a $28 loaded front-desk rate, flagged for errors in q44 and watched twice during the systems tour. The same manual step is where consent records go missing, which is not only an efficiency problem.
opportunities.blueprint: Boulevard digital intake and e-consent sent with the confirmation text, medical history written straight to the chart, consent stored against the treatment rather than in a Drive folder. Front-desk hours redeploy onto consult follow-up, which is the leak in P3.
opportunities.replaces: Printing, scanning and re-typing the intake packet; and the personal-Drive consent store that also drives the L8 finding.
